questions.q: Why did Product, Order, and Marketing consent resolve as authoritative-source decisions in a single meeting?
options: Each domain has exactly one system that clearly does that job and no other system duplicates it
Those three domains have no data at all
They were decided randomly without discussion
They required building a golden record, just like Customer
questions.explain: Atlas is the sole system that assigns SKUs and invoices orders, and Beacon is the sole system that captures marketing consent, making each an easy single-source call.

questions.q: What field is used as the match key for LTV Global's Customer golden record?
options: Email, matched case-insensitively across Atlas, Beacon, and Comet
OrderTotal
SKU
Employee ID
questions.explain: The lesson specifies Email, the same CDE defined in Lesson 5 and checked in Lesson 7, as the match key for reconciling the three customer sources.

questions.q: In the golden record's survivorship rules, which system always wins for order history, and why?
options: Atlas, because it is the only system with real, invoiced transactions
Comet, because it has the most web traffic
Beacon, because it is the CRM
Whichever system was updated most recently, with no exceptions
questions.explain: Order history is always sourced from Atlas specifically because it is the only system holding completed, invoiced transactions.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist that an authoritative-source decision be logged rather than just agreed to verbally?
options: A verbal agreement doesn't survive organizational change, so it needs to be written down with the decision, date, owners, and rationale
Logging decisions is a purely bureaucratic step with no practical benefit
Verbal agreements are legally binding and written ones are not
Only IT decisions need to be documented
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states a verbal agreement doesn't survive the next reorg, which is why the decision log captures who decided what, when, and why.

questions.q: How would the golden record approach have changed the outcome of the Lesson 1 DSAR incident?
options: It would have provided one golden Customer ID with every field traceable to its source rule, answering the request in minutes instead of six weeks
It would have made the request illegal to submit
It would have had no effect on the DSAR process at all
It would have required deleting all customer data
questions.explain: The lesson directly ties the golden record mechanism back to resolving the exact six-week delay and conflicting order histories from the Lesson 1 incident.
